author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Surviving excerpts from Origen's exegetical works on John, Matthew, and Luke, preserved in later catena and scholia collections.
argument: Origen explains why the Son is called the Word: as creator he is the divine reason through whom all things were made, and as incarnate for human salvation he is called flesh. He defends the eternal existence of the Word against those who think he began at the incarnation, and reconciles John's statement that no one receives Jesus' testimony with the fact that some do receive it. He also distinguishes 'generation' from 'birth' in Matthew, and in the Luke scholia he defends the four Gospels as the Church's approved accounts against many attempted Gospels.

outline.move: Explains why the Son is called the Word, and why John says 'was' rather than 'is' of his eternal existence.
Argues that the Word is eternal and is also called Wisdom, created as the beginning of God's ways only in relation to creation.
Resolves the apparent contradiction that no one receives Jesus' testimony though some do receive it.
Continues the resolution and explains the various senses of 'one' in Scripture.
Discusses Jesus' rebuke of the fever and whether the fever is a living being.
Brief fragment on prudence as virtue and the Lord preparing the heavens.
Distinguishes 'generation' from 'birth' in Matthew's opening, comparing the incarnate Word to spoken words written in a book.
Defends Luke's preface and the Church's selection of only four Gospels against many attempted Gospels.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He defends the eternal existence of the Word against those who think he began at the incarnation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπεί τινες τῆς ὀρθῆς πίστεως ἐκπεσόντες οἴονται ἀπὸ τότε αὐτὸν μόνον εἶναι ἀφ’ οὑ ἐκ τῆς παρθένου ἄνθρωπος γεγονὼς προῆλθεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says these people think he 'only began to be from the time he came forth as man from the virgin'—they think he only began to exist at the incarnation, not just that he 'began' in some sense. The claim understates the error: they deny his pre-existence entirely, not just think he 'began' in some qualified way.
